items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 29, 2015 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] My name is Monk Rowe... [INTERVIEWEE] I just stayed up all night long so I could make this.

ctx.x: Giacomo was interviewed in Utica, NY on March 29, 2015, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
My name is Monk Rowe and it’s 8:30 on a Sunday morning. Jazz musicians just discovered that there are two 8:30s in one day.
I just stayed up all night long so I could make this.

items.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] So for those people on YouTube, my name is Monk Rowe and this is Giacomo Gates, and we just saw you perform last night.

ctx.x: Yeah, probably was, but I’m happy to be here for the second time and I had a ball the first time.

So for those people on YouTube, my name is Monk Rowe and this is Giacomo Gates, and we just saw you perform last night. I took copious notes, so I hope you’ll analyze your own performance with great elan. It occurred to me maybe during the second or third song when you were doing vocalese, how magnificent those solos were that you and the vocalese masters set words to, that one of the ways to appreciate those solos is to listen to them with vocalese, because they are just musical gems.

I agree. I agree. The people that started to do that — Eddie Jefferson, Jon Hendricks, Annie Ross — they had great solos to choose from. People played lyrical stories, melodic lyrical stories. I’m not saying it’s easy to put lyrics to that, but the solos are just amazing. Amazing.
